desc: Sandia is the largest FFRDC in the United States by funding - approximately 4,584 million dollars in FY2024 - and it sits physically inside Kirtland Air Force Base, the same installation that contains the Manzano Weapons Storage Area and Coyote Canyon. That geography is the reason Sandia belongs on this board twice over. First, in 1948-49 the green fireballs that triggered the Los Alamos conference and Project Twinkle were concentrated over Los Alamos, Sandia and the atomic weapons installations. Second, in August 1980 the best-documented US military UFO incident of the Cold War occurred on Kirtland: AFOSI Special Agent Richard C. Doty's complaint form of 9-10 September 1980, District File No. 8017D93-0/29, records that three 1608 Security Police Squadron members - SSgt Stephen Ferenz, ATC Martin W. Rist and AMN Anthony D. Frazier - observed a bright light near the Manzano restricted test range on the night of 8 August 1980 that performed stop-and-go manoeuvres, landed in Coyote Canyon and departed vertically at high speed; and that a Sandia Laboratories security guard reported a round disc-shaped object near an alarmed structure at about 00:20 on 9 August, during which his radio malfunctioned. The same AFOSI office and the same Special Agent Doty are at the centre of the destruction of Paul Bennewitz, the Albuquerque physicist whose company Thunder Scientific sat adjacent to Kirtland and who was fed fabricated material by Air Force counterintelligence until he broke down. Sandia's laboratory security organisation appears in the AFOSI record as a reporting party. The board's reading is that Kirtland in 1980 is the clearest documented case of a contractor-operated laboratory, an Air Force counterintelligence office and a nuclear weapons storage site all appearing in the same anomalous-object incident file - and of that file being used, within months, as raw material for a disinformation operation against a private citizen.

dossier.denialPosture: The board records no denial issued by Sandia and none directed at it. That absence should be read carefully rather than charitably: the laboratory appears in the 1980 file as a reporting party, not as a respondent, and nothing here shows it was ever asked to account for what its guard saw. The deception in this story belongs to the Air Force counterintelligence office on the adjoining base, and the board keeps the attribution where the documents put it. What Sandia has not done, on any record held here, is say anything at all about August 1980.
dossier.narrative:
The 1980 file is the one to read. AFOSI Special Agent Richard C. Doty's complaint form of 9 September 1980, District File No. 8017D93-0/29, records that three members of the 1608 Security Police Squadron, SSgt Stephen Ferenz, ATC Martin W. Rist and AMN Anthony D. Frazier, observed a bright light near the Manzano restricted test range on the night of 8 August 1980 that made stop-and-go manoeuvres, landed in Coyote Canyon and departed vertically at high speed. The same file records a Sandia security guard observing a round disc-shaped object near an alarmed structure at about 00:20 on 9 August, his radio malfunctioning during the encounter.

What makes the file structurally interesting rather than merely anecdotal is that a contractor-operated national laboratory, an Air Force counterintelligence office and a nuclear weapons storage site all appear in one anomalous-object document. What makes it uncomfortable is what the same office and the same agent did next. Doty was the conduit for fabricated material supplied to Paul Bennewitz, the Albuquerque physicist whose company Thunder Scientific operated adjacent to Kirtland and who had licensed sensor technology from Sandia in 1966; the operation ended in Bennewitz's psychiatric collapse. The board grades that Tier 2 and attributes it to AFOSI, not to the laboratory.

The 2009 material is a different register and is worth keeping separate from the 1980 material. DIA memo U-429-09-DWO-IM of 30 October 2009 records the outside review of the AAWSAP deliverables, with three of the five reviewers from Sandia, and DIA recorded the reviews as positive. The board's reading of the timing is that DIA sought institutional cover for a portfolio it expected to have to defend, which it did five weeks later, and that reading is graded Tier 3 because it is an inference from sequence rather than anything the memo says.
openQuestions: The Sandia security guard of 9 August 1980 is described in the AFOSI file but the board does not hold his name, and no Sandia-side incident record from that night has been located.

The AEC-lineage custody link is the weakest thing attached to this node. It rests on a November 2025 video investigation citing Edgar Fouche and a former New Mexico state representative, and is graded Tier 2 on that basis. No primary document supports it here.
The identities of the three Sandia reviewers of the FY09 AAWSAP deliverables are not in the DIA memo as held, and nothing on this board establishes which reports they reviewed.
